blocks.text: Retrosynthesis is the opposite of synthesis. It breaks the target molecule down, on paper, into less complicated, simpler and more readily available compounds that can serve as starting materials, using the disconnection approach. The bonds disconnected are those that give a considerable structural simplification; after a series of disconnections we arrive at simple, easily available starting materials.

blocks.alt: Target Molecule on the left and Starting Material on the right, joined by two open retrosynthetic arrows pointing to the starting material. A magenta loop labelled Retrosynthesis runs over the top from the target molecule down to the starting material; a cyan loop labelled Synthesis runs round the bottom from the starting material back up to the target molecule.
blocks.caption: Figure 25.1: Synthesis and retrosynthesis routes (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 25.1).
Terms used in retrosynthesis
rows: an open-ended arrow meaning 'can be made from'
the imaginary breaking of a bond in the TM to move towards simpler starting materials
a fragment, often an ion, produced by a disconnection; a building block for the synthesis
a real reagent that does the job of a synthon, which is usually too unstable to use itself
converting one functional group into another to reach the target
a diagram of all possible disconnections and synthons from the TM back to starting materials

blocks.alt: Aniline (benzene ring with NH2), labelled Target Molecule (TM), with an open arrow labelled FGI to nitrobenzene, whose C-N bond is crossed by a wavy slash. A cyan open arrow labelled Disconnection splits into two arrows: up to synthon (A), a benzene ring with a negative charge, equivalent to benzene (SE); and down to synthon (B), NO2 with a positive charge, equivalent to HNO3, nitric acid (SE).
